One elephant seal carried a specially made electronic tag, designed to detach naturally when the animal molted.

The fourth IPY began in March 2007 and, although called a “year,” lasted for two complete years. It concluded last month after researchers from more than 60 nations completed 160 scientific projects. Organized jointly by the International Council for Science (ICSU) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the initiative was intended to advance global efforts to observe and understand the Arctic and Antarctic more effectively. Over the two-year span, the program received roughly US$1.2 billion in international funding.

“The International Polar Year 2007/2008 came at a crossroads for the planet’s future,” WMO Secretary-General Michel Jarraud said in a press statement. “The new evidence resulting from polar research will strengthen the scientific basis on which we build future actions.”

Scientists reported that during the Arctic summers of 2007 and 2008, the minimum area of permanent sea ice shrank to the smallest extent recorded since satellite monitoring began three decades earlier.

A report released in February by the IPY organizing committee said the research showed that global warming is affecting Antarctica in ways that had not been recognized before. Additional signs of climate change were gathered by IPY research ships, which detected rising temperatures in the Southern Ocean and increased ice melt producing fresher bottom water along Antarctica’s coastline.

One of the Antarctic climate-change studies was led by the Norwegian Polar Institute and focused on marine mammals. Researchers placed specially designed tags on elephant seals to track the animals’ behavior, but they later recognized that the devices could also provide valuable climate data. The tags, which dropped off when the seals molted, transmitted information about ocean temperature and salinity in waters around Antarctica, especially near the Fimbul Ice Shelf in eastern Antarctica.

Although melting ice shelves have already been observed in western Antarctica, scientists worry that similar processes may also occur in the east.

In a separate project, researchers used an autonomous robotic submarine to investigate the underside of an Antarctic glacier. A team from the United States and the British Antarctic Survey sent the “Autosub” on six missions beneath the Pine Island Glacier to study how shifts in ocean temperature were influencing the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.

Guided by sonar, the submarine navigated around the glacier and returned information that allowed scientists to build three-dimensional maps. Those maps helped them identify where and how relatively warm ocean water was melting the glacier from below.

“If [the West Antarctic Ice Sheet] were to melt completely, global sea levels would rise by as much as 5 meters,” said Stan Jacobs, the U.S. lead scientist for the project. “Because so little is known about ice-sheet behavior, this research will take us a step further in understanding how ice sheets will contribute to sea-level rise.”

**Scientists Race to Decode Polar Climate Change During International Polar Year**

*By [Reporter Name]*

As the planet warms, scientists are turning to some of Earth’s most remote and hostile regions for answers: the Arctic and Antarctic.

The International Polar Year 2007/2008, a major global research effort involving thousands of scientists from dozens of countries, is bringing renewed attention to the polar regions — places researchers say are changing faster than almost anywhere else on Earth.

The campaign, which runs from March 2007 through March 2009 to capture two full field seasons in both hemispheres, is focused on understanding how polar ice, oceans, atmosphere and ecosystems are responding to climate change — and what those changes could mean for the rest of the world.

“The poles are not isolated,” scientists involved in the project have emphasized. “What happens there affects sea level, weather patterns and ocean circulation across the globe.”

In the Arctic, researchers are tracking shrinking sea ice, thawing permafrost and changes in wildlife habitat. Satellite measurements and field expeditions are being combined to document how rapidly summer sea ice is retreating — a trend that could alter shipping routes, ecosystems and Indigenous communities that depend on ice-covered seas.

In Antarctica, attention is focused on massive ice sheets and glaciers that hold enough frozen water to significantly raise global sea levels if they melt or slide more quickly into the ocean. Scientists are particularly concerned about warming ocean water that can erode glaciers from below, weakening the ice shelves that help hold inland ice in place.

To study those hidden processes, researchers are deploying robotic submarines beneath floating ice shelves and near glacier fronts. These autonomous underwater vehicles can travel where ships cannot, measuring water temperature, salinity and currents beneath the ice. The data help scientists understand how warm ocean water reaches the base of glaciers and how quickly ice is melting from underneath.

In another innovative effort, scientists are enlisting unlikely partners: elephant seals.

The large marine mammals, which routinely dive hundreds of meters beneath the ocean surface, are being fitted with small electronic tags that record ocean conditions as the animals travel and feed. The tags collect information such as temperature, depth and salinity, then transmit the data by satellite when the seals surface.

Because elephant seals roam remote Southern Ocean waters that are difficult and dangerous for research vessels to reach, they are providing scientists with valuable data from some of the least-studied parts of the planet.

Researchers say the combination of satellites, robotic submarines, field stations, ice cores, ocean sensors and animal-borne instruments is giving them a more complete picture of polar climate systems than ever before.

The International Polar Year also marks one of the largest coordinated scientific efforts in polar history, echoing earlier polar years held in 1882-83, 1932-33 and 1957-58. But the 2007/2008 effort comes at a time of growing urgency, as evidence mounts that human-caused greenhouse gas emissions are reshaping the cryosphere — the frozen parts of Earth.

Scientists warn that polar changes could have far-reaching consequences. Melting land ice contributes to rising seas, threatening coastal cities and low-lying islands. Loss of sea ice can accelerate warming by reducing the amount of sunlight reflected back into space. Changes in the Southern Ocean and Arctic Ocean could also affect global marine ecosystems and carbon storage.

Still, researchers say the goal is not only to document loss, but to improve predictions.

By gathering data from regions that have long been gaps in climate models, the International Polar Year aims to help scientists forecast future sea-level rise, understand shifts in ocean circulation and assess risks to polar ecosystems.

For now, the work continues in some of the coldest, windiest and most isolated places on Earth — with help from satellites overhead, submarines beneath the ice and seals diving through the dark polar seas.

The message from scientists is clear: understanding the poles is essential to understanding the future of the planet.

**International Polar Year reveals accelerating change at Earth’s icy extremes**

*By [News Desk]*

The fourth International Polar Year has delivered one of the clearest assessments yet that the Arctic and Antarctic are undergoing rapid and consequential change, with major implications for global climate, sea level and ocean circulation.

The two-year scientific campaign, held in 2007–2008 and involving thousands of researchers from more than 60 countries, produced a sweeping body of observations from some of the planet’s least accessible regions. Its findings show that polar warming is outpacing global trends, Arctic sea ice is shrinking faster than expected, parts of Antarctica are losing ice, and the Southern Ocean is changing in ways that could affect climate systems worldwide.

### Polar regions warming rapidly

Scientists reported that the polar regions are proving especially sensitive to climate change. In the Arctic, temperatures have risen at roughly twice the global average in recent decades, a phenomenon known as Arctic amplification. Researchers linked this warming to the loss of reflective snow and sea ice, which exposes darker ocean and land surfaces that absorb more solar heat.

The International Polar Year also strengthened evidence that changes in the polar regions are not isolated. Warming in the Arctic influences weather patterns, ecosystems and Indigenous communities across the north, while changes in Antarctica affect global sea level and ocean circulation.

### Arctic sea ice in steep decline

One of the most striking findings was the continued decline of Arctic sea ice. During the campaign, scientists observed unusually low summer sea-ice extent, including the record minimum reached in 2007. The loss was not only in area but also in thickness and age: older, thicker multiyear ice was being replaced by younger, thinner ice that is more vulnerable to melting.

Researchers warned that the Arctic Ocean could see largely ice-free summer conditions much sooner than previously projected. The shrinking ice cover is already opening new shipping routes, increasing access to natural resources and transforming habitats for species such as polar bears, seals and walruses.

### Antarctic changes more complex, but increasingly significant

In Antarctica, the picture was more regionally varied but no less important. The Antarctic Peninsula continued to show some of the fastest warming in the Southern Hemisphere, accompanied by glacier retreat and ice-shelf collapse. West Antarctica, particularly areas draining into the Amundsen Sea, emerged as a major concern because of rapid ice loss from glaciers connected to the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.

At the same time, scientists found that the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica is changing. Observations pointed to warming in some deep and intermediate water masses, shifts in salinity and evidence that warm ocean water is reaching the undersides of floating ice shelves. This ocean-driven melting is now recognized as a key process controlling the stability of Antarctic glaciers.

The findings underscored that Antarctica’s contribution to sea-level rise could increase if warming ocean waters continue to erode ice shelves that buttress inland ice.

### Southern Ocean’s global role highlighted

The International Polar Year also improved understanding of the Southern Ocean, which plays a central role in absorbing heat and carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists reported that changes in winds, sea ice and ocean mixing may be altering the ocean’s capacity to take up carbon, with potential feedbacks to the global climate system.

Because the Southern Ocean connects the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, changes there can influence global circulation patterns. Researchers emphasized that long-term monitoring is essential to determine how these processes will evolve.

### Seals and robotic submarines transform polar research

The campaign was also notable for its innovative research methods. In Antarctica, scientists equipped elephant seals and other marine mammals with small sensors that recorded temperature, salinity and depth as the animals dived beneath sea ice. These “tagged seals” collected data from remote winter waters that ships and satellites often cannot reach, providing unprecedented observations of the Southern Ocean and the behavior of polar predators.

Another breakthrough came from autonomous underwater vehicles such as **Autosub**, a robotic submarine used to explore beneath ice shelves and sea ice. Autosub missions allowed researchers to map the underside of ice, measure ocean conditions and investigate how warm water interacts with ice shelves from below. Such technology helped fill critical gaps in areas too dangerous or inaccessible for crewed vessels.

Together with satellite measurements, aircraft surveys, drifting buoys, ice cores and ocean moorings, these tools gave scientists a far more detailed view of polar systems than was previously possible.

### A legacy of collaboration and urgency

Organized by the International Council for Science and the World Meteorological Organization, the fourth International Polar Year was the largest coordinated polar research effort in half a century. Its legacy includes new observing networks, improved climate models and expanded cooperation among scientists, governments and polar communities.

But researchers say the campaign’s most important message is one of urgency: the poles are changing faster than many earlier forecasts suggested, and those changes will be felt far beyond the Arctic and Antarctic.

“The polar regions are not remote from the rest of the planet,” scientists involved in the program concluded. “They are integral parts of the Earth system—and what happens there affects us all.”

# How Elephant Seals and Underwater Robots Helped Scientists Study Polar Climate Change

During the International Polar Year of 2007–2008, scientists faced a familiar problem: some of the most important places for understanding climate change are also among the hardest to reach. The polar oceans are cold, stormy, dark for much of the year, and often covered by sea ice. Ships can collect valuable measurements, but they are expensive to operate and cannot easily travel beneath thick ice or remain at sea throughout the winter.

To fill these gaps, researchers turned to an unusual partnership: elephant seals and autonomous underwater vehicles.

Together, these animal-borne instruments and robotic platforms helped scientists gather information from remote polar seas, improving understanding of how climate change is affecting ice, oceans, and marine ecosystems.

## The International Polar Year

The International Polar Year, often called IPY, was a major global scientific effort focused on the Arctic and Antarctic. Thousands of researchers from many countries coordinated observations of polar environments, including glaciers, sea ice, ocean circulation, atmosphere, and wildlife.

One of the major goals was to improve climate records in regions where long-term measurements were sparse. Polar regions are especially important because they play a central role in Earth’s climate system. Sea ice reflects sunlight, polar oceans absorb carbon dioxide and heat, and cold dense water formed near Antarctica helps drive global ocean circulation.

But collecting measurements in these regions is difficult. That is where new technology became essential.

## Elephant Seals as Ocean Observers

Southern elephant seals became some of the most valuable “field assistants” of the International Polar Year. These large marine mammals naturally travel thousands of kilometers through the Southern Ocean and dive repeatedly to great depths, often more than 500 meters and sometimes well over 1,000 meters.

Scientists attached small instruments to the seals’ heads, usually after the animals came ashore to breed or molt. The devices were designed to fall off later when the seals molted, minimizing long-term impact.

The tags recorded information such as:

- Water temperature  
- Salinity  
- Depth  
- Location  
- Diving behavior  

Many of the instruments were known as CTD tags, because they measured conductivity, temperature, and depth. Conductivity is used to calculate salinity, an important property for understanding ocean structure and circulation.

When a seal surfaced to breathe, the tag transmitted compressed data to satellites. This allowed researchers to receive oceanographic measurements from places and seasons that ships rarely reached, including ice-covered waters in winter.

## Why Elephant Seals Were So Useful

Elephant seals did not replace research vessels, but they extended the reach of polar science dramatically. They collected profiles of the ocean as they dived and resurfaced, creating vertical snapshots of temperature and salinity through the water column.

These measurements were especially valuable in the Southern Ocean, where winter data had been extremely limited. Ships often avoid heavy sea ice and severe storms, but seals routinely forage in these regions.

The seal data helped scientists study:

- How heat moves through the Southern Ocean  
- Where warm water approaches ice shelves  
- How sea ice influences ocean structure  
- Changes in water masses around Antarctica  
- Links between ocean conditions and seal foraging behavior  

Because elephant seals are predators, their movements also provided ecological information. Researchers could connect physical ocean conditions with where seals found food, helping build a more complete picture of polar marine ecosystems under climate stress.

## Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Beneath the Ice

Alongside animal-borne sensors, researchers also used autonomous underwater vehicles, or AUVs, to explore polar waters. These robotic vehicles can travel without a pilot onboard and can be programmed to follow specific routes, collect measurements, and sometimes map the underside of sea ice or ice shelves.

AUVs carried scientific instruments to measure properties such as:

- Temperature and salinity  
- Water currents  
- Seafloor shape  
- Ice thickness and underside roughness  
- Chemical and biological conditions  

Some AUVs operated beneath sea ice, where satellites cannot see and ships cannot easily work. Others surveyed areas near glaciers and ice shelves, where ocean warming can melt ice from below.

This was critical because one of the largest uncertainties in climate science is how quickly polar ice will melt and contribute to sea-level rise. Much of that melting occurs not from warm air above, but from relatively warm ocean water reaching the base of ice shelves and glaciers.

## Measuring a Changing Polar Ocean

The data collected by seals and AUVs helped researchers observe processes that are central to climate change.

In Antarctica, scientists are especially concerned about the interaction between the Southern Ocean and ice shelves. Ice shelves are floating extensions of the continental ice sheet. When they thin or collapse, glaciers behind them can flow faster into the sea, raising global sea level.

Ocean measurements from the IPY period helped researchers identify where warmer water masses were moving toward ice shelves and how ocean circulation could influence melting. Temperature and salinity profiles also improved estimates of ocean heat content, a key indicator of climate change.

In the Arctic, autonomous systems helped scientists examine sea ice from below. Satellite images can show the extent of sea ice, but they do not always reveal its thickness or underside structure. AUV observations helped improve understanding of how sea ice was thinning and changing in response to warming.

## Filling Gaps in Climate Models

Climate models depend on observations. Without reliable data from polar oceans, models cannot accurately represent heat transport, ice melt, ocean circulation, or ecosystem change.

The International Polar Year produced a surge of new observations, and animal-borne sensors and AUVs were part of that advance. Their data helped scientists test and improve models of:

- Sea-ice formation and melt  
- Antarctic bottom water production  
- Ocean heat transport  
- Ice-shelf melting  
- Polar ecosystem dynamics  
- Future sea-level rise  

By collecting measurements in winter and under ice, these tools addressed some of the largest blind spots in polar climate science.

## A New Era of Polar Research

The use of elephant seals and autonomous underwater vehicles during the International Polar Year showed that polar research could move beyond traditional ship-based expeditions. Instead of relying only on brief summer cruises, scientists could gather data over larger areas and longer periods, including during the harsh polar winter.

This approach also demonstrated the value of combining biology, robotics, and climate science. Elephant seals revealed conditions in places they naturally visited, while AUVs carried out targeted missions in areas too dangerous or inaccessible for humans.

The result was a richer and more detailed view of the polar oceans at a time when they were undergoing rapid change.

## Conclusion

Researchers during the International Polar Year used elephant seals and autonomous underwater vehicles to solve one of climate science’s biggest challenges: how to collect data from remote, ice-covered polar seas. Seals equipped with sensors gathered temperature, salinity, depth, and location data during their natural dives, while underwater robots surveyed beneath sea ice and near ice shelves.

Together, they provided crucial observations of warming oceans, changing sea ice, and ice-shelf melt. These measurements improved climate models and helped scientists better understand how polar regions are responding to global climate change.

In the process, elephant seals and underwater robots became unlikely but essential allies in the effort to understand Earth’s changing climate.

counterfactuals.output:
**Polar Year Findings Point to Accelerating Global Warming Risks**

*Geneva / Antarctica* — Scientists analyzing results from the 2007/2008 International Polar Year say the world’s frozen regions are showing some of the clearest evidence yet of a warming planet, with major implications for future sea-level rise.

The International Polar Year, a coordinated global research effort involving thousands of scientists from more than 60 countries, produced new observations from the Arctic, Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The findings strengthened concerns that polar warming is already reshaping ice sheets, glaciers, ocean circulation and ecosystems.

“The International Polar Year 2007–2008 came at a crossroads for the planet’s future,” said **Michel Jarraud**, then secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization. He said the research provided crucial evidence for understanding climate change and preparing for its consequences.

One of the most striking signals came from Antarctica, where researchers documented continuing losses from ice shelves and glaciers. Several Antarctic Peninsula ice shelves had already collapsed or retreated dramatically in preceding years, and IPY observations added detail on how warming air and ocean conditions weaken the floating ice platforms that help hold back land-based glaciers.

Scientists warned that the loss of ice shelves does not directly raise sea level, because the shelves already float. But their collapse can allow glaciers behind them to flow faster into the ocean, adding new water and increasing global sea levels.

Researchers also reported that parts of the **Southern Ocean** are warming, especially where relatively warm deep water reaches the edges of the Antarctic ice sheet. That process can melt ice shelves from below, thinning them and reducing their ability to restrain glaciers.

Oceanographer **Stan Jacobs**, known for his work on Antarctic ocean warming and ice-shelf melt, said observations showed the ocean playing a central role. “The ocean is delivering heat to the ice,” Jacobs said, warning that continued warming around Antarctica could increase ice loss from vulnerable regions.

Particular concern focused on West Antarctica, where large portions of the ice sheet rest on bedrock below sea level. Scientists say this makes the region vulnerable to ocean-driven melt. If major outlet glaciers there accelerate significantly, they could contribute substantially to sea-level rise over coming decades and centuries.

The IPY findings also reinforced evidence from the Arctic, where sea ice had declined sharply, permafrost was warming, and Greenland’s ice sheet was losing mass. Together, the polar observations showed that climate change was not a distant projection but an active process already visible at Earth’s extremes.

Researchers cautioned that uncertainties remain, especially about the speed of future ice-sheet response. But they said the direction of change is clear: warmer air and oceans are destabilizing polar ice, and the consequences could reach far beyond the polar regions.

Rising seas threaten coastal cities, low-lying islands, deltas and infrastructure worldwide. Even modest increases can worsen storm surges, accelerate erosion and contaminate freshwater supplies.

Jarraud said the Polar Year demonstrated the importance of sustained monitoring. Scientists involved in the effort urged governments to maintain polar observing systems, arguing that the poles act as an early-warning system for the global climate.

The message from the ice, they said, is increasingly urgent: what happens in the polar regions will not stay there.
